issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s view rests on ignoring admissible evidence or on erroneous considerations.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting the accounts of three eyewitnesses on considerations the High Court found extraneous.
The eyewitness accounts were found to be trustworthy, mutually corroborative, and supported by the first information report and medical evidence.
The High Court reappraised the evidence, identified errors in the trial court’s reasoning, and convicted the accused.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reappraise the evidence and disturb the acquittal, and its decision disclosed no error on this ground.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court has full power to review the evidence, although it ordinarily exercises caution because acquittal reinforces the presumption of innocence. The preference for an accused where two views are reasonably possible is a guideline for circumspection, not a jurisdictional limitation. A miscarriage of justice may arise from acquitting the guilty as well as from convicting the innocent. Where the trial court ignores legal and admissible evidence or adopts an erroneous view, the High Court must reappraise the evidence. The judgment refers generally to this Court’s prior pronouncements but identifies no earlier case by name; it discusses the High Court’s powers under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The matter is an appellate proceeding challenging an acquittal.

predicates.eyewitness_accounts_were_reliable: The eyewitness accounts were found trustworthy and supported by other evidence.
predicates.trial_court_used_extraneous_consideratio: The trial court rejected evidence on considerations not properly bearing on its assessment.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and the trial court ignored admissible evidence or relied on extraneous considerations, reliable evidence may support reversing the acquittal after appellate reappraisal.

issues.legal_issue: Injuries on accused persons do not, without a sufficient evidentiary basis in the circumstances, establish that they acted in private defence.
material_facts: The trial court relied on injuries to some accused persons to find that they had acted in private defence and acquitted them.
The High Court considered the sequence of events, the injuries to the deceased, the minor nature of most injuries to the accused, and the evidence identifying the accused as aggressors.
The Supreme Court held that the trial court had relied on the injuries without legal and admissible evidence establishing the claimed justification.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was wrong to treat the injuries on the accused as sufficient to justify the deaths in private defence; the High Court’s rejection of that basis was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The right of private defence under Sections 96 and 100 of the Indian Penal Code must be supported by evidence and assessed in light of the circumstances. The existence of injuries on an accused, by itself, does not establish that the accused were entitled to cause death in private defence.

predicates.criminal_case_involving_private_defence: The criminal proceeding concerns a claim that the accused acted in private defence.
predicates.accused_had_injuries: One or more accused persons had injuries.
predicates.circumstances_identified_accused_as_aggr: The surrounding circumstances showed that the accused initiated or carried out the attack.
predicates.no_evidence_established_justifying_defen: No legal and admissible evidence established that the accused were justified in using the force claimed.

issues.definition: In a criminal case involving private defence, injuries to the accused do not establish the defence where the circumstances identify them as aggressors and no evidence otherwise justifies the force used.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may share a common object without prior concert or a prior meeting of minds, and members may be liable for an offence committed in pursuit of that object when the relevant facts establish the shared object and the offence’s connection to it.
material_facts: The accused were on inimical terms with the complainant party, and their hostility had been aggravated by litigation over the disputed trees.
The accused came to the scene armed with deadly weapons and attacked the complainant party together.
The attack resulted in three deaths, and the circumstances showed that the participants shared the object pursued in the attack.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in finding that the accused involved in the occurrence shared a common object and in applying liability for acts committed in its prosecution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code does not require prior concert or a meeting of minds. Common object is inferred from the attending facts and circumstances. A concerted attack by a group armed with deadly weapons may support an inference that the participants shared an object that included an offence known to be likely in its prosecution. Mere presence as an innocent bystander is not enough; the circumstances must establish membership and the shared object.

predicates.common_object_liability_case: The criminal proceeding concerns whether participants in an unlawful assembly share liability for an offence committed by members of the group.
predicates.group_attack_with_deadly_weapons: The participants carried out a concerted attack while armed with deadly weapons.
predicates.participants_shared_an_identical_interes: The circumstances showed that the participants shared an interest pursued through the assembly and attack.
predicates.offence_was_likely_in_pursuit_of_that_ob: The offence was one the participants knew was likely to be committed in pursuit of their shared object.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about common-object liability, members who share an interest in a deadly-weapon group attack may be liable for an offence committed in pursuit of that object when the offence was likely in its pursuit.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that some accused were not identified is not a basis for excluding them where the first information report names them and eyewitnesses repeat those identifications in court.
material_facts: The first information report named all the accused as participants in the attack.
The eyewitnesses identified the accused in their trial testimony, and the Supreme Court found their accounts cogent and reliable.
The defence argued that some accused had not been named, but the record did not support that contention.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the claim that some accused should be acquitted because their names were absent from the first information report or the trial testimony.
issues.legal_principle: The identification of accused persons in the first information report and reliable repetition of those identifications in court may defeat a claim that particular accused were not named. The Court applied this principle to the evidence in the record and cited no earlier case by name.

issues.definition: In a criminal group-attack case, accused persons named in the initial report and reliably identified by eyewitnesses in court are not excluded for lack of identification.

issues.legal_issue: The first information report need not name every witness, and a witness’s testimony is not discredited merely because the witness was not named in that report.
material_facts: One eyewitness was not named in the first information report.
That eyewitness was injured and was related to a deceased person, and the High Court found the witness to be a natural witness of the occurrence.
The Court stated that the report’s purpose is to set the criminal law in motion and that the law does not require all witnesses to be named in it.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the eyewitness’s name from the first information report did not justify rejecting the testimony.
issues.legal_principle: There is no requirement that the first information report name all witnesses; its object is to set the criminal law in motion. The Court cited no earlier case by name in stating this principle.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_witness_testimo: The criminal proceeding relies on testimony from a witness to the occurrence.
predicates.witness_was_not_named_in_initial_report: The witness’s name was omitted from the initial report of the occurrence.
predicates.witness_was_a_natural_witness: The circumstances showed that the witness was naturally present at or able to observe the occurrence.

issues.definition: When a natural witness testifies in a criminal case, omission of the witness’s name from the initial report does not by itself justify rejecting the testimony.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to a deceased person is not, by itself, a reason to discard the witness’s testimony.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses were related to the deceased, and one eyewitness was injured in the occurrence.
The High Court found the witnesses’ presence at the scene established and their accounts trustworthy and corroborative.
The Court held that their relationships to the deceased did not justify rejecting their evidence.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationships to the deceased were not a ground to discard their testimony.
issues.legal_principle: A witness’s relationship to a deceased person, by itself, is not a sufficient ground for rejecting testimony. The Court considered the witnesses’ presence, the circumstances of the occurrence, and the reliability of their accounts; it cited no earlier case by name for this proposition.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_eyewitnesses: The criminal proceeding relies on eyewitness testimony to establish the occurrence.
predicates.witnesses_were_related_to_deceased: The eyewitnesses were related to a person who died in the occurrence.
predicates.witnesses_were_natural_and_credible: The witnesses’ presence was natural in the circumstances and their testimony was found credible.

issues.definition: In a criminal case relying on eyewitnesses, their relationship to the deceased does not by itself justify rejecting their testimony when their presence was natural and their accounts were credible.
